body.p: This paper provides a useful assessment of the role of macrophages in the development of functional paw withdrawal, which is a feature in the mouse model of vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy (VIND). The authors present solid data suggesting a role for E-selectin as a critical molecule promoting VIPN, acting via immune cell recruitment and inflammasome-mediated signalling; however, the role of NLRP3 in this model is based on in vitro assays. This study will be of interest for immunologists.

The authors have included a number of written edits to their manuscript that improves the readability of the text and also provides clarity on their experiments and findings. Together these changes better highlight the role of E-selectin as an upstream driver of innate immune inflammation in vincristine-induced neuropathy.

A comment I made in the first review round (previous comment #3) was that NLRP3-inhibitors were only used in vitro and not used in vivo to confirm that it is this specific innate immune complex that contributes to the pathway. Instead, the downstream inflammatory mediator IL-1b was inhibited in vivo using anakinra (and not tested in vitro). The authors have referred to their previous work on NLRP3 inhibitors in their vincristine model and modified some text to delineate that in vivo, only a role for IL-1b was investigated in the E-selectin experiments in the current paper. It would be useful to clearly distinguish throughout the text, that the role of NLRP3 was only confirmed in macrophages in vitro. E.g. lines 44, 87, 740 and 773 discuss their findings on NLRP3 in macrophages, but do not specify that this is in vitro data.
MCC950 is also known as CP-456773 and CRID3, which would be helpful to mention the first time the inhibitor is introduced as all versions of the name are used in current publications.
Summary:

This is an interesting mechanistic study on the topic of Vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy (VIPN). It defines E-selectin as critical molecule of promoting VIPN, acting via immune cell recruitment and inflammasome-mediated signalling.
Using antibody treatments, genetic models and in vitro studies, the authors convincingly show that E-Selectin is a driver of VIPN.
Strengths:
In vivo studies are robust and useful. Antibody studies as well as the inflammasome-related work are very well done.
The following is the authors’ response to the original reviews.

We thank the Reviewing Editor and both reviewers for their careful evaluation of our manuscript. We appreciate the reviewers’ recognition of the strength of the in vivo studies and of the evidence identifying E-selectin as a driver of vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy (VIPN).

In revising the manuscript, we have focused on clarifying the experimental rationale, strengthening the connection between the different experimental systems, providing additional methodological detail, and ensuring that our conclusions accurately reflect the scope of the data. In particular, we have clarified the distinction between (i) the established requirement for NLRP3–IL-1β signalling in VIPN, demonstrated previously using genetic and pharmacological approaches, and (ii) the new mechanistic question addressed here: whether E-selectin functions upstream of this pathway by regulating macrophage recruitment and amplifying inflammatory signalling.

disp-quote.p: (1) The initial experimental paradigm looks at the DRG neurons, which are located by the spine, and from there the foot pad is examined in subsequent experiments. It would be relevant to show whether the foot pad is altered in the vincristine-treated mice and whether the infiltration of myeloid cells that was demonstrated at DRGs is also observed in the foot in the vincristine model. Otherwise, the mechanism being investigated in the vincristine model, which might have similar functional results (paw withdrawal), but the mechanism behind both could be completely different.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this point. We have revised the manuscript to clarify the anatomical relationship between the tissues examined and the distinct purpose of the intraplantar E-selectin experiment.

The cell bodies of primary sensory neurons innervating the hind paw are located in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG). Their axons travel within peripheral nerves, including the sciatic nerve, and terminate as sensory endings in the plantar skin. Thus, the DRG, sciatic nerve and footpad represent different compartments along the same peripheral sensory pathway. Examining the DRG and sciatic nerve therefore assesses inflammation surrounding the somatic and axonal compartments of the sensory neurons whose peripheral terminals mediate withdrawal responses from the hind paw.

Following systemic vincristine administration, we observed increased F4/80-positive immune-cell accumulation in both the DRG and sciatic nerve. This response was attenuated by pharmacological blockade or genetic deletion of E-selectin, demonstrating E-selectin-dependent inflammation at multiple sites along the peripheral sensory pathway. We also assessed the footpad for structural neuropathy following repeated systemic vincristine treatment and found no significant loss of intraepidermal nerve fibres. However, we did not quantify F4/80-positive cells in the footpad following systemic vincristine and therefore cannot determine from the present study whether immune-cell accumulation also occurs around the peripheral sensory terminals.

Importantly, the mechanistic relationship between systemic and local vincristine administration has previously been examined directly in our laboratory. Both systemic intraperitoneal and local intraplantar vincristine produced mechanical allodynia (Starobova et al., 2021; PMID: 33656514, Starobova et al., 2019; PMID: 31316337). Hypersensitivity induced by either route was attenuated by disruption of the TLR4-NLRP3–IL1β pathway, including genetic deletion of Tl4r or Nlrp3 and, e.g. pharmacological inhibition of NLRP3 with MCC950. These findings demonstrate that systemic and intraplantar vincristine converge on a shared NLRP3-dependent neuroimmune mechanism, despite the different initial distribution of vincristine exposure.

The intraplantar E-selectin experiment in the present study was designed to determine whether E-selectin is sufficient to initiate immune-dependent hypersensitivity locally within the peripheral tissue innervated by DRG neurons. Intraplantar administration restricts exposure to one hind paw, allowing the local effects of E-selectin to be distinguished from its systemic endothelial functions. Local E-selectin administration caused unilateral mechanical hypersensitivity and increased F4/80-positive immune-cell accumulation in the injected footpad. This response required functional E-selectin ligands and was attenuated by depletion of phagocytic cells. In addition, E-selectin promoted the adhesion of bone marrow-derived macrophages but not DRG neurons. Together, these findings demonstrate that locally presented E-selectin is sufficient to recruit or retain phagocytic cells and produce hypersensitivity in the peripheral territory of DRG neurons.

We have revised the Discussion to explain this anatomical and experimental relationship. We now clarify that the intraplantar E-selectin paradigm tests the local sufficiency of E-selectin-dependent immune signalling rather than reproducing the precise anatomical distribution of inflammation following systemic vincristine.

“Primary sensory neurons innervating the hind paw have their cell bodies in the DRG, axons within peripheral nerves including the sciatic nerve, and sensory terminals in the plantar skin. Analysis of these tissues therefore examines distinct compartments along the same peripheral sensory pathway. Systemic vincristine increased F4/80-positive immune-cell accumulation in both the DRG and sciatic nerve, demonstrating inflammation surrounding the somatic and axonal compartments of peripheral sensory neurons. Although we did not quantify immune-cell accumulation in the footpad following systemic vincristine, repeated systemic treatment caused no detectable loss of intraepidermal nerve fibres. Moreover, previous work directly comparing systemic and intraplantar vincristine demonstrated that both routes produce mechanical allodynia through a shared NLRP3–IL1β-dependent mechanism, with hypersensitivity attenuated by Nlrp3 deletion or pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition with MCC950 [8,18].”

“The intraplantar E-selectin paradigm used here was designed to determine whether E-selectin is locally sufficient to induce immune-dependent hypersensitivity within the peripheral territory innervated by DRG neurons. Intraplantar administration restricts E-selectin exposure to one hind paw, allowing its local effects to be distinguished from its systemic endothelial functions. Local E-selectin administration caused unilateral mechanical hypersensitivity and increased F4/80-positive immune-cell accumulation in the injected footpad, with both responses dependent on functional E-selectin ligands and phagocytic cells. Together with the preferential adhesion of bone marrow-derived macrophages rather than DRG neurons to E-selectin, these findings demonstrate the local sufficiency of E-selectin-dependent immune signalling. This paradigm should therefore be interpreted as a mechanistic sufficiency experiment rather than as an anatomical reproduction of systemic VIPN.”

disp-quote.p: (2) The rationale of performing spatial sequencing on DRG neurons isolated from vincristine mice is unclear. It is likely that more information could have been obtained from looking at sections from these animals, and there would be a better link to the experiments on BMDMs which follow afterwards. Indeed, the spatial data does not seem to play a key role in the study. There is not a clear link between it (which was carried out on DRGs) and the later focus on macrophages and indeed the NLRP3 inflammasome.

body.p: We appreciate this comment and regret if the rationale linking the spatial transcriptomic analysis to the subsequent mechanistic experiments was insufficiently explicit.

We first note an important clarification: spatial transcriptomics was not performed on isolated DRG neurons. Intact DRG sections containing neuronal, immune, Schwann-cell, fibroblast, pericyte and other cellular populations were analysed using Visium spatial transcriptomics followed by SPOTlight deconvolution. The experimental design specifically preserved the multicellular DRG environment.

The rationale arose directly from the preceding experiments. Despite robust mechanical hypersensitivity and increased F4/80-positive immune-cell accumulation, we observed no detectable loss of intraepidermal or myelinated fibres. We therefore used spatial transcriptomics to ask whether functional neuropathy was associated instead with molecular stress and altered communication between neuronal and non-neuronal cells, and whether these responses were modified by E-selectin blockade/deletion. This rationale is already reflected in the Results but has now been made more explicit.

Importantly, the spatial analysis provides the bridge to the macrophage experiments rather than representing an independent component of the study. The analysis identified immune and stromal populations as prominent signalling hubs, while sensory-neuron populations predominantly occupied receiver roles. Furthermore, E-selectin deletion suppressed inflammatory/interferon-associated transcripts predominantly within immune-cell populations. These observations motivated the subsequent reductionist experiments examining whether E-selectin directly modifies macrophage inflammatory signalling. We have revised the Results accordingly:

“Given the absence of detectable structural nerve damage despite robust mechanical hypersensitivity and immune-cell accumulation (Fig. 2E–H), we used spatial transcriptomics of intact DRG sections to identify molecular signatures of neuronal stress and altered multicellular signalling underlying VIPN. This approach also enabled us to determine how genetic deletion or pharmacological blockade of E-selectin alters these responses and to identify the cellular compartments most affected by E-selectin perturbation. DRGs were collected following a single vincristine (0.5 mg kg-1, i.p.) or saline injection from C57BL/6J mice, Sele-/- mice, and C57BL/6J mice pre-treated with E-selectin-neutralising antibody, and analysed for gene-expression changes and spatial signalling patterns.”

disp-quote.p: (3) The authors suggest that the E-selectin is enhancing NFkB-induced priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome. LPS+vincristine increased IL-1b release from BMDMs in vitro, which was elevated in the presence of E-selectin. E-selectin also increased ASC speck formation by approx. 20% in vitro. The ASC speck formation in vitro was blocked by MCC950, a specific NLRP3 inhibitor, but the authors went on to use anakinra in vivo using the E-selectin i.pl model. It is really unclear why the switch to anakinra occurred for the in vivo work, as blocking IL-1b is central to many inflammatory pathways, not just NLRP3. Use of MCC950 would have been more appropriate to demonstrate that negative effects on mechanical function are mediated by the NLRP3 inflammasome. As there were no readouts of NLRP3 inflammasome activity measured in any of the mice in vivo (e.g. local ASC specks, IL-1b release, western blot of typical inflammasome components such as IL-1b, caspase-1, ASC or gasdermin D) either at the DRG site or the foot, we cannot say that the cell culture data mimics or models the in vivo conditions at this time.

body.p: We agree with the reviewer that anakinra establishes a requirement for IL-1 signalling, rather than uniquely identifying NLRP3 as the upstream source of IL-1β in the intraplantar E-selectin model. We have therefore revised the manuscript to avoid interpreting the anakinra experiment alone as evidence of NLRP3 activation in vivo.

However, we respectfully note that the role of NLRP3 in vincristine-induced neuropathy itself has already been established directly in our previous work. Starobova et al. demonstrated that vincristine-induced mechanical allodynia and gait abnormalities are prevented in Nlrp3-/- mice and attenuated by systemic MCC950 treatment, and that anakinra prevents VIPN. This study additionally established macrophages as the source of NLRP3-dependent IL-1β in this model (Starobova et al., J Exp Med, 2021; PMID: 33656514), and that anakinra prevents mechanical hypersensitivity that occurs downstream of NLRP3 activation via Il1b release.
The purpose of the current study was therefore not to re-establish whether NLRP3 is required for VIPN, but to identify an upstream regulator of this previously established pathway.
The present experiments provide several complementary pieces of evidence:
(1) E-selectin adhesion enhances ASC-speck formation in vincristine-treated macrophages.
(2) This enhancement is completely abolished by MCC950.
(3) E-selectin increases IL-1β release under the same conditions.
(4) E-selectin enhances NF-κB p65 activation.
(5) E-selectin-induced mechanical hypersensitivity is attenuated by IL-1 receptor blockade with anakinra.
(6) E-selectin-adhered, LPS+VCR-treated macrophages produce greater hypersensitivity when transferred into the paw than equivalently treated control-adhered macrophages.
The ASC-speck/MCC950 and IL-1β experiments are already reported in the manuscript.

We agree, nevertheless, that without direct measurement of ASC specks/caspase-1/GSDMD in the E-selectin intraplantar model, the manuscript should not state that this experiment independently demonstrates NLRP3 activation in vivo.
We have therefore changed wording such as:
“E-selectin-mediated enhancement of NLRP3-driven IL-1β release contributes to the development of VIPN in vivo.”
to the more precise:

“E-selectin amplifies NLRP3-dependent IL-1β release from vincristine-stimulated macrophages in vitro, while IL-1 receptor signalling contributes to E-selectin-induced mechanical hypersensitivity in vivo”
We also added a paragraph to discussion:

“Although previous genetic and pharmacological studies establish NLRP3 as a critical mediator of VIPN [8,14], NLRP3 activation was not directly measured in vivo following local E-selectin administration in the present study. Thus, our in vivo data establish dependence on IL-1 receptor signalling, whereas the specific amplification of NLRP3 activation by E-selectin is demonstrated directly in macrophages.”

disp-quote.p: (4) Additionally, the reliance on the E-selectin administration models for the second half of the paper is curious. It would have been relevant to test whether the immune-modulating inhibitors could also attenuate the vincristine-induced effects on mechanism hypersensitivity, to better link the E-selectin model with the vincristine one.

body.p: We agree that this connection should be made clearer. However, the requested experiment has, in large part, already been performed and published.

The purpose of the present study was to define how E-selectin is mechanistically linked to VIPN. A critical first question was whether E-selectin could contribute to hypersensitivity through a direct effect on sensory neurons. This cannot readily be resolved within the systemic vincristine model because vincristine has multiple concurrent effects on sensory neurons, immune cells and the vasculature, making it difficult to isolate any direct neuronal effect specifically attributable to E-selectin. Intraplantar administration provided the clearest functional test because it exposes peripheral sensory terminals, where sensory transduction occurs, directly to E-selectin and permits measurement of the resulting unilateral mechanical response. Combining this approach with phagocyte depletion and IL-1 receptor blockade allowed us to determine whether E-selectin-induced hypersensitivity persisted in the absence of immune-cell signalling. Electrophysiological studies in dissociated DRG neurons could provide complementary information, but in the absence of a defined neuronal target or predicted electrophysiological effect, it is unclear which parameters would provide a definitive test.

Our results support an immune-mediated rather than direct sensory neuron mechanism. E-selectin promoted adhesion of bone marrow-derived macrophages but not DRG neurons. Moreover, intraplantar E-selectin produced unilateral mechanical hypersensitivity and increased F4/80-positive immune-cell accumulation in the injected footpad, while E-selectin-induced hypersensitivity was attenuated by phagocyte depletion and IL-1 receptor blockade with anakinra. Thus, even when E-selectin is administered directly into tissue containing peripheral sensory terminals, its effect on mechanical sensitivity depends predominantly on immune cells and downstream IL-1 signalling.

Having established this, the second objective was to determine how E-selectin-dependent immune activity is linked to sensory hypersensitivity in VIPN. The downstream immune-modulating experiments proposed by the reviewer have already been conducted in the vincristine model. In our earlier study, macrophage depletion prevented vincristine-induced neuropathy; NLRP3 deficiency prevented vincristine-induced mechanical allodynia and gait abnormalities; MCC950 attenuated VIPN; and IL-1 receptor blockade with anakinra prevented VIPN (Starobova et al., 2021; PMID: 33656514).
Repeating these experiments would therefore not independently test a new biological question.

Instead, the present study determines how E-selectin intersects with this established macrophage–NLRP3–IL1β pathway. We demonstrate that pharmacological blockade or genetic deletion of E-selectin prevents vincristine-induced mechanical hypersensitivity and reduces F4/80-positive immune-cell accumulation in the DRG and sciatic nerve, directly establishing a requirement for E-selectin in the systemic vincristine model. We then show that E-selectin adhesion enhances vincristine-induced NF-κB activation, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and IL1β release in macrophages, with inflammasome activation abolished by MCC950. Finally, the finding that anakinra attenuates intraplantar E-selectin-induced hypersensitivity demonstrates that E-selectin and vincristine converge functionally on IL-1 receptor signalling in vivo.

Together, the previous and present studies interrogate successive components of the same mechanism. The earlier work established that macrophages and NLRP3–IL1β signalling are required for vincristine-induced neuropathy. The present study demonstrates that E-selectin is required for vincristine-induced immune-cell accumulation and hypersensitivity, acts predominantly through immune cells rather than directly on sensory neurons, and enhances vincristine-induced NLRP3–IL1β signalling in macrophages. The intraplantar E-selectin experiments therefore provide a mechanistic bridge between E-selectin-dependent immune activity and sensory hypersensitivity rather than representing a separate model unrelated to VIPN.
We have revised the Discussion to make the rationale for these experiments and their mechanistic connection to the systemic vincristine model explicit.
We have now explicitly connected the two studies in the Discussion:

“These findings extend our previous demonstration that macrophage depletion, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of NLRP3, and IL-1 receptor antagonism protect against vincristine-induced neuropathy [8,14]. Here, we sought to define how E-selectin is mechanistically linked to this established macrophage–NLRP3–IL1β pathway and to sensory hypersensitivity. A critical component of this question was whether E-selectin acts directly on sensory neurons or indirectly through immune cells. Intraplantar administration exposed peripheral sensory terminals directly to E-selectin while permitting assessment of a local, unilateral mechanical response. However, E-selectin promoted macrophage but not DRG neuron adhesion, and E-selectin-induced hypersensitivity was attenuated by phagocyte depletion and IL-1 receptor antagonism. These findings support a predominantly immune-mediated mechanism rather than direct sensitisation of sensory neurons.”

“Together with the protection afforded by E-selectin blockade or deletion in the systemic vincristine model, our findings position E-selectin at the point of convergence between immune-cell recruitment and inflammatory signalling in VIPN. E-selectin facilitates macrophage accumulation within peripheral neuronal tissues while also enhancing vincristine-induced NF-κB activation, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly and IL1β release. E-selectin thereby couples immune-cell recruitment and activation to IL1R-dependent sensory hypersensitivity.”

disp-quote.p: (5) Details are missing from the figure legends and the methods. The concentrations of compounds used in cell culture and exposure times are not clear.

body.p: We thank the reviewer and acknowledge that including these details in the figure legends rather than only the methods section improves clarity. The Supplementary Methods specify that BMDMs were primed with LPS (10 ng/mL) for 3 h, followed where indicated by MCC950 (10 μM; 30-min pretreatment), vincristine (100 μM; 6 h), doxorubicin (50 μM; 6 h), cyclophosphamide (100 μM; 6 h), or nigericin (5 μM; 45 min). E-selectin, P-selectin and IgG-coated surfaces were used at 5 μg/mL.

We have revised the legends for Figures 4–6 and Supplementary Figure S5 to specify the concentrations and exposure times for all relevant in vitro treatments, including LPS, vincristine, nigericin, MCC950, doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide, as well as the concentrations used for E-selectin, P-selectin and control-coated surfaces. These additions ensure that the experimental conditions can be understood directly from the corresponding figures.

disp-quote.p: The spatial transcriptomics data need to be improved in terms of visualization. The authors should plot genes that define the cell types in the sequencing dataset, and also show the cellular map on the cut, not only UMAPs. Can the authors not use the n=3 samples per condition to perform some statistical analyses? While the CellChat analyses are informative, they are difficult to read. Fold change over control when comparing conditions and pathways may be a better way of visualization.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions and have clarified the presentation, statistical analysis and rationale of the spatial transcriptomic experiments.

First, the n=3 biological replicates per condition were already used for statistical inference. Visium barcodes originating from each individual animal were aggregated to generate one pseudobulk count matrix per animal, thereby avoiding pseudoreplication of individual spatial spots. Differential expression was analysed using DESeq2 with a negative binomial model including batch as a covariate, followed by Wald testing and Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Differentially expressed genes were defined as adjusted P<0.05 and |log2FC| ≥0.585. We have revised the Methods and Results to make clearer that the three animals per condition represent independent biological replicates and that individual Visium spots were deliberately not treated as independent replicates.

Second, cell populations were inferred using SPOTlight against an annotated single-cell RNA-seq reference. We have clarified the reference-guided annotation strategy and expanded the description of the defining neuronal and non-neuronal populations. The objective of the spatial analysis was not to generate a new DRG cell atlas, but to determine how vincristine-induced transcriptional responses are distributed across DRG cellular compartments and how these responses are altered by genetic or pharmacological perturbation of E-selectin.

Importantly, the transcriptional responses identified here are consistent with several independent transcriptomic analyses of DRG following vincristine treatment. Our previous bulk RNA-seq study identified 368 differentially expressed genes following vincristine treatment, with cell-type and gene-set enrichment analyses demonstrating predominant effects on immune-system-associated genes (Starobova et al., 2020; PMID: 31260808). An independent study by Bernard et al. similarly identified substantial transcriptional changes in DRG following systemic vincristine, including inflammatory/immune and neuronal injury-associated processes (Bernard et al., 2022; PMID: 36559317). More recently, transcriptomic profiling of peripheral nervous tissue following vincristine alone and as part of the CVAD combination regimen demonstrated distinct, time-dependent and treatment-specific neuroimmune responses, with vincristine contributing prominently to the inflammatory phenotype (Starobova et al., 2026; PMID: 42294786). Together, these independent datasets support a reproducible vincristine-induced transcriptional response involving neuroimmune and neuronal stress pathways. The present spatial analysis extends these bulk-transcriptomic findings by resolving these responses across neuronal, immune, Schwann-cell and stromal compartments and determining how they are altered by E-selectin perturbation.

Finally, we acknowledge that CellChat networks are information-dense. However, CellChat communication probabilities are model-derived measures of predicted intercellular signalling and are not directly equivalent to conventional gene-expression fold changes. Expressing these values as fold change over control could therefore imply a quantitative interpretation that is not appropriate for this analysis. We have consequently retained the pathway-specific sender/receiver/mediator/influencer representation and clarified the methodological basis and interpretation of the CellChat communication probabilities in the Methods.

“To ensure that statistical inference was performed at the level of independent biological replicates rather than individual Visium spots, barcodes originating from the same animal were aggregated to generate one pseudobulk count matrix per animal (n = 3 biological replicates per condition). Individual Visium spots were not treated as independent biological replicates.”

“Cell-type composition of Visium spots was inferred using seeded non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) regression-based deconvolution implemented in SPOTlight (v1.8.0) [29]. A harmonized cross-species single-cell RNA-seq dataset containing previously annotated neuronal and non-neuronal DRG populations was used as the reference [30]. Gene expression and metadata from the spatial transcriptomics dataset were used to construct a SpatialExperiment object, and marker-gene profiles from the reference clusters were used to generate cell-type-specific topic profiles. These profiles were projected onto individual Visium spots to estimate the relative contribution of each cell population. Thus, cell-type assignments represent reference-guided estimates of cellular composition rather than single-cell measurements and were used for spatial visualization and downstream cell-type-resolved analyses.”

“Cell–cell communication analysis was performed using CellChat [31]. The merged spatial Seurat object was split by condition to generate separate CellChat objects, and ligand–receptor interactions were inferred using the mouse secreted signalling database. Communication probabilities were calculated using the tri-mean method, with interactions involving fewer than 10 cells excluded. Pathway-level communication networks were inferred and aggregated to compare signalling strength and interaction numbers across cell types. For selected pathways, CellChat-derived communication probabilities and network centrality metrics were used to identify predominant sender, receiver, mediator and influencer populations and contributing ligand–receptor interactions. As CellChat communication probabilities are model-derived measures integrating ligand and receptor expression across interacting cell populations, they represent predicted relative communication strength rather than conventional gene-expression values and were therefore not interpreted or presented as gene-expression fold changes between conditions.”

disp-quote.p: In Figure 1B, the % DAB is not easy to understand. It would be better to do the staining also via IF, and then maybe to count nuclei. The corresponding figures shown in the supplemental figure are not convincing. If F4/80 is not working well, Iba1 could be an alternative.

body.p: We thank the reviewer and agree that the original label “% DAB” did not adequately describe the quantitative endpoint. We have clarified the Methods and figure legend and changed the axis label to “F4/80-positive area.”

The endpoint represents the percentage of analysed tissue area occupied by DAB-positive F4/80 immunoreactivity. It is not intended to represent the percentage of macrophages or the percentage of nuclei that are F4/80 positive. Quantification of immunoreactive area and counting of labelled cells are alternative approaches to assessing macrophage accumulation, each with distinct advantages and limitations. Because F4/80 is expressed on the cell membrane and within the cytoplasm rather than the nucleus, nuclear counting would require additional staining and reliable assignment of individual nuclei to irregularly shaped F4/80-positive profiles. This can be particularly difficult in densely stained or morphologically complex tissue and would not necessarily provide a more accurate measure of macrophage burden.

The detection and quantification method was selected to suit the endpoint. Chromogenic F4/80 immunohistochemistry provides permanent, spatially resolved staining that can be quantified across a defined tissue area using consistent thresholding. In our experience, immunofluorescence in formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded neuronal tissue can introduce additional sources of variability, including tissue autofluorescence, background signal and sensitivity to imaging parameters. Changing to immunofluorescence would therefore alter the detection method without necessarily improving the biological measurement.

Similarly, replacing F4/80 with Iba1 would introduce a different marker with a different expression profile rather than validate the same endpoint. The F4/80 assay used here produced specific and quantifiable staining, included appropriate isotype controls, and was performed using a previously optimised and validated protocol. Quantification was conducted by a blinded observer using an automated image-analysis workflow. We have therefore retained the established DAB-based F4/80 assay and clarified throughout the manuscript that the reported measure is F4/80-positive tissue area rather than macrophage number.

“F4/80 staining was performed using a previously optimised and validated immunohistochemical protocol for mouse DRG [8,24,25]. Sections were stained with rat anti-mouse F4/80, developed using ABC/DAB, counterstained with haematoxylin, scanned, and quantified by a blinded observer using Visiopharm. Representative images are provided in Supplementary Figure S1.”

“Fig. 1. Inhibition of E-selectin and VCAM-1, but not other adhesion molecules, attenuates vincristine-induced mechanical hypersensitivity and increased F4/80-positive area in the dorsal root ganglia and sciatic nerves. Effects of blocking antibodies against VCAM-1 (VCAM1ab; A, B), ICAM-1 (ICAM1ab; C, D), PECAM-1 (E, F), P-selectin (P-sel ab; G, H) and E-selectin (E-sel ab; J, K) on vincristine-induced mechanical hypersensitivity (A, C, E, G, J; PWT, paw withdrawal threshold) and F4/80-positive area in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and sciatic nerve (SN) (B, D, F, H, K). Black arrows indicate i.p. administration of blocking antibodies (10 mg/kg), isotype control antibodies (IgG2b or IgG1; 10 mg/kg) and vincristine (0.5 mg/kg). VCAM-1 and E-selectin blockade attenuated vincristine-induced mechanical hypersensitivity (A, J) and the associated increase in F4/80-positive area in the DRG and SN (B, K), whereas PECAM-1 and P-selectin blockade was partially effective (E–H) and ICAM-1 blockade had no effect (C, D). F4/80-positive area was quantified as the percentage of analysed tissue area occupied by thresholded DAB-positive F4/80 immunoreactivity and does not represent the percentage or number of F4/80-positive cells. Data are presented as mean ± SEM (n = 5–7 per group). Statistical significance (#P < 0.05) was determined using repeated-measures two-way ANOVA or one-way ANOVA with Šídák’s multiple-comparisons test.”

disp-quote.p: The authors should define the background of all the mice used. Have they been back-crossed to B6j mice? One cannot compare C57BL6J mice with full knockouts if they are not littermate controls. Especially immunological responses are completely dependent on the background of mice. See, e.g. PMID: 40568896.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point and have now clarified the genetic background and provenance of all mouse lines in the Methods. The Sele-/- and Fut4-/-/Fut7-/- lines were maintained on a C57BL/6 background. These strains have previously been reported to have been backcrossed onto the C57BL/6 background for at least 10 generations (Barbier et al., 2020; PMID: 32341362), and Fut4-/-/Fut7-/- mice have independently been characterised on a C57BL/6 background (Wang et al., 2013; PMID: 23562273). The ASC-citrine reporter line was generated and characterised as described by Tzeng et al. (2016; PMID: 27346360).

We acknowledge that age-matched C57BL/6J mice, rather than littermate wild-type controls, were used for the knockout comparisons, and this has now been stated explicitly in the Methods. We therefore interpret the genetic experiments together with the complementary pharmacological experiments. Importantly, the phenotype observed in Sele-/- mice is independently supported by E-selectin-neutralising antibody experiments performed entirely in C57BL/6J mice, which similarly attenuated vincristine-induced mechanical hypersensitivity and the associated increase in F4/80-positive area. Thus, the pharmacological experiments provide an independent same-background line of evidence supporting the contribution of E-selectin to vincristine-induced neuropathy.

“Behavioural and in vivo experiments were performed using 8–10-week-old male C57BL/6J, E-selectin-deficient (Sele-/-), fucosyltransferase 4/7 double-knockout (Fut4-/-Fut7-/-), and ASC-citrine reporter mice. The Sele-/- and Fut4-/-Fut7-/- lines were maintained on a C57BL/6 background and have previously been reported to have been backcrossed onto this background for at least 10 generations [15]. The C57BL/6 background of Fut4-/-Fut7-/- mice has also been independently reported [16]. ASC-citrine reporter mice were generated and characterised as previously described [17].”

Although the genetic studies used age-matched C57BL/6J rather than littermate controls, the protective phenotype observed in Sele-/- mice was independently recapitulated by pharmacological E-selectin blockade in C57BL/6J mice, supporting an E-selectin-dependent mechanism while reducing the likelihood that the findings are attributable solely to genetic-background effects.

disp-quote.p: Could the authors comment on the role of ICAM2? Why was this not tested as well?

body.p: We thank the reviewer for raising ICAM-2. Our initial panel was designed to sample major inducible endothelial adhesion pathways implicated in inflammatory leukocyte recruitment, including selectins and members of the immunoglobulin superfamily. ICAM-2 was not included because its endothelial regulation and function differ from those of ICAM-1, VCAM-1 and E-selectin. ICAM-2 is constitutively expressed on endothelial cells and participates predominantly in leukocyte adhesion/transendothelial migration, while inflammatory cytokines can decrease rather than increase endothelial ICAM-2 expression (PMID: 10223354; PMID: 10574717).
We agree, however, that absence of ICAM-2 testing means that the manuscript should not imply that all relevant endothelial adhesion molecules were comprehensively excluded.
“By examining representative members of major vascular adhesion-molecule families, we …”

Additionally, ICAM-2 was not examined in the present study. Unlike inducible ICAM-1 and E-selectin, ICAM-2 is constitutively expressed on endothelial cells and has context-dependent roles in leukocyte transmigration; inflammatory cytokines can reduce endothelial ICAM-2 expression [42,43]. Thus, although our results identify E-selectin and VCAM-1 among the adhesion molecules tested, they do not exclude contributions from ICAM-2 or other endothelial adhesion pathways.
